subject: Geography
sub_topic: Glacial erosion vs glacial deposition landforms

concepts.name: Glacial Erosion Processes: Abrasion vs. Plucking (Quarrying)
key_dimensions: Mechanical distinction: abrasion smoothens/polishes while plucking fractures and removes joint blocks
Role of basal sliding velocity and pressure melting in determining dominance of each process
UPSC trap: both occur simultaneously but produce different landform signatures (striations vs. craggy surfaces)
Link to rock type and jointing pattern — why plucking dominates in well-jointed rocks

concepts.name: Cirque (Corrie/Cwm): Formation and Diagnostic Features
key_dimensions: Processes involved: nivation, rotational flow of ice, freeze-thaw, abrasion and plucking together
Morphological features: bergschrund crevasse, rock lip/threshold, tarn lake formation after deglaciation
UPSC trap: cirque is an erosional landform but the tarn lake within it is often confused with depositional origin
Asymmetry of cirques on poleward vs. equatorward slopes and implications for aspect-controlled glaciation

concepts.name: Arête and Horn (Pyramidal Peak): Formation Logic and Distinction
key_dimensions: Arête formed by back-to-back erosion of two adjacent cirques — a knife-edged ridge
Horn (e.g., Matterhorn) formed by erosion from three or more cirques converging — distinction from arête critical for MCQs
UPSC trap: both are erosional landforms but students often misclassify horn as depositional due to 'pyramid' shape
Real-world examples: Matterhorn (Horn), Aiguille (Arête) — useful for map-based questions

concepts.name: Glacial Trough (U-shaped Valley): Formation and Associated Features
key_dimensions: Transformation from V-shaped river valley to U-shaped glacial trough by abrasion and plucking on valley floor and walls
Parabolic cross-section vs. true U-shape — UPSC trap on exact shape description
Associated features: truncated spurs, hanging valleys, ribbon lakes (rock basin lakes) — all part of the same erosional system
Distinction from rift valleys (tectonic) which may appear U-shaped — a classic UPSC overlap trap

concepts.name: Hanging Valley and Waterfalls: Differential Erosion Concept
key_dimensions: Formed when a tributary glacier has less erosive power than the main glacier, leaving tributary valley floor elevated
Post-glaciation: tributary rivers cascade as waterfalls into the main trough (e.g., Yosemite Falls)
UPSC angle: explains why some of the world's highest waterfalls are in formerly glaciated regions
Distinction from river-cut gorges — hanging valleys are uniquely glacial and reflect ice volume disparity

concepts.name: Roche Moutonnée: Asymmetry as an Erosion Process Indicator
key_dimensions: Stoss (up-ice) side: smooth and polished by abrasion; Lee (down-ice) side: rough and jagged from plucking
Critical UPSC trap: can determine direction of past ice movement from asymmetry — a common application-based question
Distinction from drumlin (depositional): both are elongated but roche moutonnée is bedrock erosion while drumlin is till deposit
Size range and occurrence in bedrock outcrops — useful to distinguish from crag-and-tail

concepts.name: Crag-and-Tail: Erosion-Deposition Hybrid Landform
key_dimensions: Hard rock crag on up-ice side shields softer material on lee side, forming a tail of till or softer rock
UPSC trap: it is a combined erosional (crag) and depositional (tail) landform — not purely one category
Edinburgh Castle Rock is the classic example — useful for statement-based questions
Distinction from roche moutonnée: crag-and-tail involves differential rock resistance while roche moutonnée is in uniform bedrock

concepts.name: Striations, Grooves, and Polished Surfaces: Micro-Erosional Evidence
key_dimensions: Formed by rock fragments embedded in basal ice scraping bedrock — direct evidence of past glaciation
Orientation of striations reveals ice movement direction — palaeoglaciology application
UPSC trap: striations are erosional micro-features often confused with tectonic lineaments in map questions
Difference between striations (fine lines), grooves (deeper channels), and chatter marks (crescent-shaped)

concepts.name: Fjords: Glacial Troughs Invaded by Sea
key_dimensions: Formed by glacial over-deepening of coastal valleys below sea level, subsequently flooded after deglaciation
Characteristic shallow threshold/sill at mouth — formed where glacier entered the sea and erosion decreased
UPSC trap: fjords are erosional in origin but are often confused with rias (river valleys drowned by sea — not glacial)
Global distribution: Norway, Chile, New Zealand, Alaska — important for physical geography map questions

concepts.name: Types of Moraines: Lateral, Medial, Terminal, and Ground
key_dimensions: Lateral moraine: debris along sides of glacier from valley walls; Medial: formed by merging of two lateral moraines
Terminal (end) moraine marks maximum advance of glacier; Recessional moraines mark successive retreat stages
UPSC trap: ground moraine (till plain) is often confused with outwash plain — ground moraine is unsorted, outwash is water-sorted
Push moraine vs. dump moraine — distinction based on whether ice was actively advancing or stagnating

concepts.name: Drumlins: Formation Controversy and Diagnostic Features
key_dimensions: Elongated, streamlined hills of till with steep stoss end (up-ice) and gentle lee end — opposite asymmetry to roche moutonnée
Formation theories: subglacial deposition under moving ice, erosion of pre-existing till deposits — still debated
UPSC trap: drumlin orientation indicates ice movement direction (blunt end points up-ice) — same application as roche moutonnée but for depositional context
Drumlin fields (basket of eggs topography) — distinction from esker fields which form linear ridges

concepts.name: Eskers: Subglacial Meltwater Deposition
key_dimensions: Long, sinuous, narrow ridges of stratified sand and gravel deposited by meltwater streams flowing within or beneath glacier
UPSC trap: eskers are depositional but formed by meltwater (fluvioglacial), not direct ice deposition — a hybrid process
Beaded eskers form where subglacial streams periodically expanded into cavities — seasonal variation indicator
Distinction from moraines (unsorted till) and kames (mound form) — all three are depositional but differ in process and form

concepts.name: Kames and Kame Terraces: Ice-Contact Depositional Forms
key_dimensions: Kames: irregular mounds of stratified sand and gravel deposited by meltwater in contact with stagnant ice
Kame terraces: flat-topped benches formed by meltwater streams flowing between glacier and valley wall
UPSC trap: kame terraces resemble river terraces morphologically but have different origin — a classic identification question
Kame-and-kettle topography — combination of kames and kettle holes forming an irregular landscape

concepts.name: Kettle Holes and Kettle Lakes: Dead Ice Topography
key_dimensions: Formed when blocks of stagnant dead ice buried in outwash sediment melt, causing surface collapse
Result in enclosed depressions which may fill with water to form kettle lakes (e.g., Minnesota lake district)
UPSC trap: kettle lakes are depositional-process-related but the depression itself is formed by removal (melting), not addition
Distinction from tarns (formed in cirques by erosion) and ribbon lakes (formed in glacial troughs) — all post-glacial lakes but different origins

concepts.name: Outwash Plains (Sandur): Fluvioglacial Deposition
key_dimensions: Formed by braided meltwater streams depositing sorted, stratified sediment beyond the terminal moraine
Sorting characteristic: coarser material near glacier, finer material (varved clay) further away — graded bedding
UPSC trap: outwash plains are water-sorted (stratified) unlike ground moraine (unstratified till) — a frequently tested distinction
Valley sandur vs. piedmont sandur and their link to proglacial lake formation

concepts.name: Varves and Proglacial Lakes: Seasonal Sediment Record
key_dimensions: Varve: a pair of sediment layers (coarse summer layer + fine winter layer) deposited annually in proglacial lakes
Used in varve chronology to date deglaciation events — geochronological tool
UPSC trap: varves are found in glacial lake sediments, not in moraines or outwash plains — location specificity matters
Distinction from loess (wind-deposited glacial flour) — both are fine-grained glacial products but deposition mechanism differs

concepts.name: Glacial Erratics: Evidence of Past Ice Movement and Extent
key_dimensions: Boulders transported by glaciers far from their source rock and deposited in geologically alien locations
Used to reconstruct past glacial flow paths and extent of ice sheets — palaeoglaciology application
UPSC trap: erratics are depositional features but their VALUE lies in erosional source area identification — dual utility
Famous examples: Precambrian erratics in Britain from Scandinavia — used in map/statement questions on glacial extent

concepts.name: Till vs. Fluvioglacial Sediments: Sorting as the Key Diagnostic
key_dimensions: Till: directly deposited by ice — unstratified, unsorted, angular to sub-angular clasts of mixed size (diamicton)
Fluvioglacial sediments: deposited by meltwater — stratified, sorted, rounded clasts
UPSC trap: both are glacial in origin but the sorting/stratification distinction is the critical separator in MCQs and statements
Lodgement till (deposited under moving ice) vs. ablation till (deposited from melting surface) — further subdivision

concepts.name: Glacial vs. Periglacial Landforms: Boundary Confusion
key_dimensions: Periglacial landforms (pingos, patterned ground, solifluction terraces) form in cold climates without direct glaciation
UPSC trap: periglacial loess deposits and glacial outwash are both found in same regions but have wind vs. water origin respectively
Pingo (ice-cored hill) often confused with drumlin — both are hills in cold regions but entirely different genesis
Relevance to India: Himalayas have both glacial (erosional troughs, moraines) and periglacial (rock glaciers, patterned ground) landforms

concepts.name: Indian Himalayan Glacial Landforms: Applied Context for UPSC
key_dimensions: Major glaciers: Siachen, Gangotri, Zemu — location, associated landforms and their erosional/depositional classification
Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs): link between moraine-dammed proglacial lakes and disaster risk — policy angle
UPSC trap: retreating glaciers expose both erosional (polished bedrock, striations) and depositional (fresh moraines) features simultaneously
Kedarnath disaster 2013 — chorabari lake (moraine-dammed) breach — integration of glacial geomorphology with disaster management
